title: Homework Week 10
intro: Three questions from the **CJMC 2024** paper — **B04, B05 and C02** — plus **C05** as an optional challenge. Do them on paper first, then check here. After each one, open “Play with it”.

questions.text: Two runners, Joy and Hope, run around a square (ABCD) with side lengths of 200 m.
hints: Do they run **towards** each other or in the same direction? When runners come towards each other, add their speeds.
How far apart are they at 9:00 along the way they are heading towards each other? After the first meeting, how much *more* distance must they cover together to meet again?
Together they cover 75 + 125 = 200 m every minute. First meeting: 600 m ÷ 200. Next meeting: one whole lap of 800 m later.

traps.0: 9:06 would be “twice as long as the first meeting”. But the second meeting comes after they have together covered **one more lap (800 m)** — that takes 4 minutes after the first meeting, not 3.
traps.2: 9:08 assumes the first meeting is after 4 minutes (800 ÷ 200). But at the start they are only **600 m** apart the way they are running towards each other, so the first meeting is at 9:03.

solution: Joy runs A → D → C → B and Hope runs B → C → D → A, so they run **towards** each other.
The way they are heading towards each other, Joy at A and Hope at B are 600 m apart (A → D → C → B). Together they close the gap at 75 + 125 = **200 m/min**.
To meet a second time they must together cover one whole lap: 800 ÷ 200 = **4 min** later → 3 + 4 = 7 min → **9:07** → **(B)**.
questions.idea: Running towards each other: **add the speeds**. A repeat meeting needs one extra whole lap between them.

questions.text: Grandma is sewing a traditional Indigenous design typically found on blankets and elsewhere, called a star-blanket design, on a tapestry. The pattern is made up of **200 rhombi**.
hints: “Each edge” means each little line segment **once**, even though two rhombi may share it.
Each rhombus has 4 sides. If nothing were shared, how many sides would there be? Then think: shared edges got counted twice.
Count the edges on the **outside** of the star (counted once) — 8 points, each with 2 outside sides of 5 small edges.

traps.4: 80 m = 200 × 4 × 10 cm counts every rhombus’s four sides separately, so every shared edge is counted **twice**. Edges between two rhombi should only be sewn once.

solution: The star is 8 big diamonds, each a 5 × 5 block of small rhombi: 8 × 25 = 200 ✓.
200 rhombi × 4 sides = **800** sides. An edge **between** two rhombi is counted twice; an edge on the **outside** only once.
Outside edges: 8 points × 2 sides × 5 small edges = **80**.
questions.idea: Add up all the sides, then fix the double counting: shared edges are counted twice.

questions.text:
The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 can be placed in the circles below with each number used exactly once and such that the sum of the three numbers in the circles on each side of the square is the same for all sides.
**What is the largest possible value that sum can take?**
hints: The 4 corner circles belong to **two** sides each; the 4 middle circles belong to only one side.
Add the four sides: every number is counted once, **corner numbers twice**. So 4 × (side sum) = 36 + (sum of the corners).
To make the side sum as big as possible, the corners should be big. But 4 × (side sum) has to be a multiple of 4. What are the biggest corners that work?

traps.4: A side sum of 16 would need the corners to add to 4 × 16 − 36 = 28. The four biggest numbers only add to 8 + 7 + 6 + 5 = 26, so 16 is impossible.

solution: Let S be the side sum. Adding all 4 sides counts every number once and every **corner twice**: 4S = 36 + (corners).
Corners add to at most 8 + 7 + 6 + 5 = 26, so 4S ≤ 62, so S ≤ 15 (S is a whole number).
Can S = 15? Then the corners add to 4 × 15 − 36 = 24. Try corners 3, 8, 6, 7 (clockwise) with middles 4, 1, 2, 5: 3 + 4 + 8 = 15, 8 + 1 + 6 = 15, 6 + 2 + 7 = 15, 7 + 5 + 3 = 15 ✓.
So the largest possible sum is **15** → **(D)**.
questions.idea: Count how many times each position is used, build an equation, then bound it (largest corners) and test the best case.

questions.text:
A 6-digit number is said to be “exciting” if it satisfies each of the following properties.
  • Each of the digits 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 occur exactly once;
  • The number formed by the first *n* digits is divisible by *n*, for each *n* = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
For example, 987654 is exciting because 9 is divisible by 1, 98 is divisible by 2, 987 is divisible by 3, 9876 is divisible by 4, 98765 is divisible by 5, and 987654 is divisible by 6.
**Not including 987654, how many exciting numbers exist?**
hints: Sam’s hint: **keep on using the divisibility rules.** Start with the strictest clue — the first 5 digits must be divisible by 5. What can the 5th digit be (using only 4–9)?
Divisible by 2, 4 and 6 means the 2nd, 4th and 6th digits are even. Which even digits do you have? Then use “digit sum divisible by 3” for the first three digits.
After the 5th digit = 5 and evens in places 2, 4, 6 → places 1 and 3 hold 7 and 9. The 2nd digit must make 7 + 9 + ? divisible by 3.

traps.2: There are exactly **two** exciting numbers, but one of them is the example 987654 — and the question says “not including 987654”.

solution: **5th digit:** the first 5 digits must be divisible by 5, so they end in 0 or 5 → the 5th digit is **5**.
**Evens:** the 2nd, 4th and 6th digits must be even (divisible by 2, 4 and 6). The even digits are 4, 6, 8 — so they fill places 2, 4, 6 and the 1st and 3rd digits are **7 and 9**.
**2nd digit:** 7 + 9 + ? must be a multiple of 3 → 16 + 8 = 24 → the 2nd digit is **8**.
**4th digit:** the 3rd and 4th digits must make a number divisible by 4: 76 ✓ (96 ✓), so the 4th digit is 6 and the 6th digit is 4.
The only exciting numbers are 789654 and 987654. Not counting the example: **1** → **(B)**.
questions.idea: Start with the clue that leaves the **fewest choices** (divisible by 5 → ends in 5) and build up one place at a time.
